prompt:
Deep-ocean bioluminescence: "Abyssal Lanterns". We are hovering in the open water column far below the surface at night. The water is an almost-black indigo that deepens to pure ink at the bottom, with the faintest teal haze high up where moonlight barely reaches; a few very soft, slowly swaying light shafts fall from the top edges of the frame and fade out before mid-screen (keep the top-centre clock area dark and calm — the shafts belong at the sides).

Life: 5–9 original, abstract bioluminescent creatures — translucent bell-shaped drifters with long, gently trailing filaments (not any real species, not any cartoon). Each glows a soft cyan, aquamarine or violet core with a faint halo, pulses very slowly (breathing period 6–12 s, never a flash), and drifts on its own gentle curved path, rising and sinking over minutes so they never pile up or leave. Their filaments follow behind with a delayed, wavy motion. Size them from lp.min so they read well on a 16:10 laptop and stay small and elegant on a 32:9 ultra-wide; spread them across the whole width (on 32:9 the far left and right thirds must be just as alive as the centre).

Atmosphere: three depth layers of drifting "marine snow" (tiny pale specks sinking slowly and swaying, the far layer dimmer, smaller and slower — real parallax), and every 20–40 s a soft wave of tiny blue-green plankton sparks that ripples across part of the screen along a curved line and fades out over several seconds, as if a current brushed past. Depth fog: far creatures are dimmer and bluer.

Mood: hypnotic, quiet, premium, mostly very dark with luminous accents — a lock screen seen in a dark room. No flashes, no fast motion, no text.

Craft: the picture must be a pure function of lp.t (no simulation in update()), loop-free but stable for hours (wrap phases). Pre-render the water gradient, light shafts and a dither layer in resize(); draw creatures' glows with cached glow sprites (LivePaper.util.glow / glowSprite), batch the snow into a few Path2D fills per layer, draw fewer particles when lp.quality < 1. Aim for ≤ 2 ms per frame at 1512x982@2 and well under 150 mW in the battery profile. Check the stills at 32:9, 16:10, 5:4, the 320x200 thumbnail and t=600 and make every one look composed and beautiful.
summary:
"Abyssal Lanterns" is finished and passes the full `livepaper check` with no problems: about 1.55 ms per frame at 1512×982@2 and 1.77 ms at 5120×1440, 106 mW on the battery profile, and brightness behind the clock of only 14–18/255.

We hover in dark indigo water that fades to pure ink at the bottom, with a faint teal haze up high. A few soft moonlight shafts fall from the top corners, sway slowly and fade before mid-screen, so the area around the clock stays dark. Between five and nine abstract, lantern-like translucent bells drift there, more of them on wider screens, spread evenly to the far edges. Each glows soft cyan, aquamarine or violet with a faint halo. Each one breathes on its own 6–12 s cycle, squeezing gently and brightening a little, and rises and sinks along a curved path over several minutes. Their filaments and oral arms trail behind on a delay, with slow ripples running down them. Distant creatures are smaller, dimmer and bluer. Three layers of marine snow sink and sway at different speeds and dim with depth. Every 20–40 s a curved wave of tiny blue-green plankton sparks lights up across part of the screen and fades out over several seconds.

The picture depends only on time, so it looks the same at any moment and stays stable for hours. One thing I found: the built-in colour-mix helper returns a format the glow helpers can't read, which made every creature render grey-white. The scene now uses its own mixer.

The manifest `id` is still the template's "quiet-aurora", because the instructions said to leave it unchanged.

prompt:
Art-director notes — this is already lovely; refine it to excellent. Keep the palette, darkness, the calm clock area and the performance.

1. Variety of life: all creatures currently share one silhouette (the same dome with a scalloped rim, similar size), so the frame reads a bit like a set of icons. Give them 3–4 distinct, still original body types: a tall bell, a flat wide disc with a fringe of very fine tentacles, a small round one with two long ribbon-like frilly arms, and an elongated comb-jelly-like drifter (an oval with faint shimmering rows of light along its sides). Vary sizes much more: one or two large, near, dimmer and slightly softer creatures (partly allowed to cross the frame edge), several mid-size, and a few tiny distant ones.
2. Living motion: make the bell pulse visibly deform the body (contract narrower and taller, relax wider) with the glow brightening gently on each contraction, and let the tentacles lag and curl in response. Keep it slow (6–12 s cycles).
3. Vertical composition: right now the creatures sit in a band through the middle. Spread them over the full height (except the clock area), with a sense of depth (far ones higher up and fainter, near ones lower and larger is fine).
4. Glow: let the luminous cores and rims carry a slightly stronger, soft halo so they read as real light in the dark (the frame is very dark at 11–13/255 — a little more luminous accent is welcome; stay well under the clock budget).
5. The background shows a faint regular dot-grid at small sizes (clearly visible in the 320x200 thumbnail) — probably the dither tile repeating. Make the dither irregular/finer so no pattern is visible at any size.
6. Keep the plankton spark waves (they look great in the thumbnail) and make sure one is visible at some of the sampled times on the large stills too.

Check all stills (32:9, 16:10, 5:4, thumbnail, t=600) before you finish.
summary:
The refined "Abyssal Lanterns" passes the full check. Frame time is 2.4 ms at 1512×982@2 and 3.3 ms at 5120×1440, against budgets of 4 and 6 ms. Brightness is 14–20/255 overall and 14–19/255 behind the clock (limit 120), with no JS errors. I looked at all 13 stills: 16:10, 32:9, 5:4, the thumbnail and t = 600.

The scene is a deep night ocean with faint moonlight shafts, drifting marine snow and four kinds of glowing creature:
- **Tall bells** with long tentacles and short central arms.
- **Flat wide discs** with a fringe of very fine tentacles.
- **Small round drifters** trailing two long, frilly ribbon arms.
- **Oval comb-drifters** with rows of light that shimmer along their sides as the body slowly turns.

**Depth and layout:** tiny, faint, fog-tinted creatures sit high and far away, mid-size ones are spread over the full height, and one or two large, dim, softer ones (two on ultra-wide screens) drift low and partly off the edge. Placement spreads them out and keeps the clock area clear at every screen shape.

**Motion:** every 6–12 s each bell contracts quickly, narrower and taller, and rises slightly. It then relaxes slowly to wider, and its glow brightens on each contraction. The tentacles follow the creature's own movement a few seconds late, flaring and curling in response.

**Glow:** cores and rims have a stronger soft halo, and the frame is a little brighter than before (14–20/255, was 11–13).

**Dither:** the background grain is now finer and irregular, so the dot grid in the thumbnail is gone.

**Plankton waves:** one now sweeps past about every 30 s, timed so a wave shows in the large 30, 90, 240 and 600 s stills.

Two things came out differently from your notes:
- **The large near creatures are dimmer, not truly blurred.** A real blur pass cost about 2 ms per frame, so I dropped it. They're drawn with fainter, wider lines and a weaker outline instead.
- **The ribbon arms are subtler than the other new features.** At current sizes they read as two twisting, wavy strands rather than broad ribbons. I can make them wider if you'd like them to stand out more.

I also updated the scene description in `scene.json`.

prompt:
Excellent progress — the variety of creatures, the comb jelly's light rows, the big soft near jelly and the plankton waves are exactly right. One last refinement round; keep everything else as it is:

1. Journeys: comparing the stills at t = 30, 240 and 600, every creature stays near the same spot (it only wobbles), so after a few minutes on the lock screen the composition never changes. Give each creature a slow journey instead: rising (most) or sinking across the whole height over 3–8 minutes each (different speeds per depth: far ones slower), with a gentle sideways meander, leaving the frame at one edge and re-entering at the other (fade in/out near the edges so nothing pops). Stagger them so the frame always holds roughly the same number of creatures, spread out (no clumping). It must remain a pure function of lp.t (e.g. y = wrap(phase + t * speed)), deterministic, and stable for hours.
2. Clock area: creatures may pass through the top band, but fade any creature to ~25 % opacity while it is inside lp.clockRect (expanded by a margin) so the clock stays clean.
3. The large near jelly: as it travels it should drift across the frame too, not stay parked at the right edge; keep it soft and dim.

Check the JPEG previews in scene/.check/previews/ at t = 30, 240 and 600 to confirm the composition actually changes over time while staying balanced.
summary:
The full check passes: 2.4 ms per frame at 1512×982 against a 4 ms budget, 3.4 ms on the ultra-wide against 6 ms, no JavaScript errors, and the area behind the clock stays dark (about 15–20 out of 255, limit 120). The t = 30, 240 and 600 previews now show clearly different, still balanced layouts, and so do the 32:9 and 5:4 frames.

Abyssal Lanterns still shows the same bells, fringed discs, frilly-armed ribbon drifters and comb jellies with their travelling rows of light, now moving on slow journeys through the dark water. Each depth layer has its own pace: far creatures take about 7½ minutes to cross the screen, mid-depth ones about 5, and the large near jelly about 3⅓. Most rise, and one creature in the far and mid layers sinks. Each creature fades in at one edge, crosses the full height with a gentle sideways meander, fades out at the other edge and comes back on a slightly different line. Within each layer the creatures are evenly spaced in time and each has its own column, with neighbours in time kept far apart sideways. That keeps the count on screen roughly constant and stops creatures in the same layer from bunching up, though one layer can still pass in front of another. Any creature passing behind the clock dims smoothly to about 25 % and brightens again as it leaves. The big, soft, dim near jelly now drifts diagonally across the whole frame, changing direction on each crossing, instead of staying parked at the right edge. Everything is still a pure function of time, so the scene is repeatable and stable for hours. The marine snow, moonlight shafts and plankton waves are unchanged.

I also added a few creatures to the far and mid layers, since each one is now off screen for part of its journey, and updated the description in `scene.json` to mention the journeys.
